{{Short description|Mathematical knot}}
{{more citations needed|date=May 2014}}
[[Image:Blue Figure-Eight Knot.png|thumb|upright|[[Figure-eight knot (mathematics)|Figure-eight knot]] ''is'' fibered.]]

In [[knot theory]], a branch of [[mathematics]], a [[knot (mathematics)|knot]] or [[link (knot theory)|link]] <math>K</math>
in the [[3-sphere|3-dimensional sphere]] <math>S^3</math> is called '''fibered''' or '''fibred''' (sometimes '''Neuwirth knot''' in older texts, after [[Lee Neuwirth]]) if there is a 1-parameter family <math>F_t</math> of [[Seifert surface]]s for <math>K</math>, where the parameter <math>t</math> runs through the points of the [[unit circle]] <math>S^1</math>, such that if <math>s</math> is not equal to <math>t</math>
then the intersection of <math>F_s</math> and <math>F_t</math> is exactly <math>K</math>.

==Examples==
===Knots that are fibered===
For example:

* The [[unknot]], [[trefoil knot]], and [[figure-eight knot (mathematics)|figure-eight knot]] are fibered knots.
* The [[Hopf link]] is a fibered link.

===Knots that are not fibered===
[[File:Blue Stevedore Knot.png|thumb|upright|The [[Stevedore knot (mathematics)|stevedore knot]] is ''not'' fibered]]
The [[Alexander polynomial]] of a fibered knot is [[monic polynomial | monic]], i.e. the coefficients of the highest and lowest powers of ''t'' are plus or minus&nbsp;1. Examples of knots with nonmonic Alexander polynomials abound, for example the [[twist knot]]s have Alexander polynomials <math>qt-(2q+1)+qt^{-1}</math>, where ''q'' is the number of half-twists.<ref>{{cite journal|arxiv=dg-ga/9612014 |title=Knots, Links, and 4-Manifolds |last1=Fintushel |first1=Ronald |authorlink1=Ronald Fintushel| last2=Stern |first2=Ronald J. |authorlink2=Ronald J. Stern| journal=[[Inventiones Mathematicae]] |volume=134 |year=1998|issue= 2|pages=363–400|doi=10.1007/s002220050268|mr=1650308 }}</ref> In particular the [[Stevedore knot (mathematics)|stevedore knot]] is not fibered.

==Related constructions==
Fibered knots and links arise naturally, but not exclusively, in [[complex algebraic geometry]].  For instance, each [[Mathematical singularity|singular point]] of a [[complex plane curve]] can be described 
topologically as the [[cone (topology)|cone]] on a fibered knot or link called the '''link of the singularity'''.  The [[trefoil knot]] is the link of the [[Cusp (singularity)|cusp singularity]] <math>z^2+w^3</math>; the Hopf link (oriented correctly) is the link of the [[Singular point of a curve|node singularity]] <math>z^2+w^2</math>.  In these cases, the family of [[Seifert surface]]s is an aspect of the [[Milnor fibration]] of the singularity.

A knot is fibered if and only if it is the binding of some [[open book decomposition]] of <math>S^3</math>.
